newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE cool on Albania force but backs aid.
newsitem.headline: OSCE cool on Albania force but backs aid.

text.p: Ambassadors of Europe's top security body agreed on Thursday that the OSCE should assist Albania in shoring up democracy but found no consensus for sending a stabilisation force to the chaos-torn Balkan state.

The permanent council of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) backed a recent report of the OSCE's special envoy Franz Vranitzky, but appeared to backtrack on its initial enthusiasm for the former Austrian chancellor's call for urgent foreign intervention.

The Vienna-based body held an emergency meeting on Saturday at which member states expressed broad support for proposals made by Vranitzky after his talks with Albanian leaders, including the idea of sending an outside force to the country.
"While the idea of a force is still in the air, we have seen no consensus for having such a force," an OSCE spokeswoman said, noting the situation in Albania had since become calmer.

EU states have ruled out military intervention in Albania. The head of an EU fact-finding mission to Albania said on Thursday the Union's first priority should be to help restore order and provide a safe passage for food aid.
This could involve a "modest (European) police presence" which could take the form of police or military advisers, Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg said.
But the EU called on Albania to ensure the conditions, with regard to law and order, for outside assistance to be provided.
The OSCE said it was ready to work with other institutions to rebuild democratic institutions in Albania and pave the way for fresh elections scheduled for June, which it would also monitor.

"The main thing is we have an agreement of 54 countries for a big OSCE effort in Albania," the spokeswoman said. "The OSCE will prepare the ground for elections, which will be an important political move -- to bring about a government that everyone supports."
The OSCE groups most of Europe with the United States and Canada.
Albania descended into anarchy after citizens went on the rampage, enraged by the loss of their life savings in collapsed bogus pyramid schemes.
However, there was some semblance of normality in the capital on Thursday after the airport reopened for business.
The OSCE statement noted that most of its recommendations had already been followed, including a dialogue between all parties and the establishment of a broad-based government.
The body said it was also prepared to consider monitoring the collection of weapons in Albania.
Vranitzky will continue in his role as OSCE special envoy to Albania, the organisation said.
